title: How to stop videos from autoplaying in Chrome on Mac: what works and what doesn't
metaTitle: Stop Autoplay Videos in Chrome on Mac: Steps That Work
description: How to stop videos from autoplaying in Chrome on Mac: block sound per site, and why muted videos still start. Steps for macOS 13 and later.
targetKeyword: how to stop videos from autoplaying in chrome on mac
intro: Google's own help pages do not describe a switch that stops autoplay for every site. What you can do is turn off sound for each site in Chrome's Site settings, but a muted video will still start.
tldr: Chrome on Mac has no documented switch that stops autoplay on every site.
For one site, open the icon left of the address, choose Site settings, then change Sounds.

blocks.text: Autoplay is when a video starts before you press play. You open an article, a clip starts, and the sound jumps out before you find the tab. Most people want the sound off first. Many also want the video to stop starting on its own. Chrome handles those two wishes differently, so it helps to know which one you can fix.
What Chrome on Mac can and cannot block

Chrome gives you control over sound, not over starting. The Sounds setting in Site settings decides whether a site can play audio. Google's Chrome Help page describes it that way. The same page does not mention autoplay, and it does not name a Mute option. That gap explains why older guides and newer ones describe different menus.

Chrome's developer documentation has the detail that matters most. Muted autoplay is always allowed. A site can start a video with the sound off. Blocking audio will not stop the picture from moving. Google's developers describe the autoplay policy in their blog, and they document no switch for users.
Turn off sound for one site in Chrome

Start with the site that annoys you most. Open it in Chrome first, so the address bar shows its address. The per-site controls apply only to the site you are on. Changes save automatically, so there is no Save button to look for. Then follow the steps in this guide to reach the Sounds control.

Labels will not always match what you see. Google's help page uses the name Sounds. Third-party guides describe Mute and Automatic (default) options, but Google does not confirm those names. Read the choices in the menu. Then pick the one that stops the site from playing audio.
Why a muted video still starts

Chrome's autoplay rules decide what a video can do on its own. Chrome 66 tightened autoplay for audio and video elements in April 2018. Under those rules, muted autoplay is always allowed. Autoplay with sound needs one of a few conditions. The list below shows them.

items: You have interacted with the site first.
The site has crossed the desktop Media Engagement Index threshold.
The site is an installed PWA on desktop.

blocks.text: The engagement rule explains why some sites get sound after a while. Chrome counts a playback toward a site's index only in certain cases. The playback must last over 7 seconds. It needs unmuted audio, an active tab, and a video larger than 200x140 px. Chrome's developer blog states those limits.
Check a site's engagement score

Chrome lets you view your own index. Click the address bar, type about://media-engagement, and press Return. The page is for viewing. This guide does not use it to block anything. Treat what you see as a clue about a site, not as a switch.
Stop autoplay on every site

No documented setting stops autoplay across every site at once. You have a few routes, and each covers something different. The per-site Sounds setting covers audio. The site's own player may cover the start. Muting a tab covers only the sound. Pick the route that fits the site, then test it.

items: Per-site Sounds: blocks audio on that one site. Repeat it for each site.
The site's own player: some video sites show an autoplay control near the play button.
Muting the tab: silences sound, but the video keeps playing.
A Chrome extension: some guides name Disable HTML5 Autoplay. Its status is unverified.

blocks.title: Check an extension first
blocks.text: Extensions can read the pages you visit, depending on the permissions they ask for. Before you install one, read its listing, its permissions, and its recent reviews. I could not confirm that Disable HTML5 Autoplay is still maintained, so treat it as unverified.

blocks.text: Permission prompts and what the buttons mean

Some sites ask to use a feature, and Chrome shows a permission prompt. Google's help page lists three choices: Allow this time, Allow while visiting the site, and Never allow. Use Allow this time for a single use. Use Never allow when you want that feature blocked for the site.
Mistakes people make

The most common mistake is following an old guide. A Macworld article from September 21, 2017 covers macOS Sierra and High Sierra. It relies on Flash and on a Chrome > Preferences menu. Current Chrome uses More > Settings, so skip any step that sends you to Preferences.

Another mistake is trusting mute as a fix. Muting silences the sound, but the video still plays on screen. Stopping the picture is a different job, and the options for it are limited. Test a video for at least a few seconds before you decide the setting works.
A third mistake is testing too early. Reload the tab after you change the setting. A page that is already playing may still reflect the old state. Then start the video again and listen for sound.
Requirements and versions

Chrome on Mac requires macOS 13 Ventura or later. Google's system requirements page gives that minimum but gives no date for it. On an older release, current Chrome will not run. Update macOS first, then return to these steps.

I could not confirm the current stable Chrome version from an official page during research, so this guide names no version number. Menu labels here follow Google's help pages. If your window shows different wording, pick the closest match and keep going.
Next steps if a video still plays sound

Start with the one site that bothers you. Confirm that Sounds now blocks audio for it. Reload the tab and play the video again. If sound still comes through, check whether the site's own player or an extension is causing it. Then repeat the same steps for the next site on your list.

faq.question: Is there a setting that turns off autoplay for every site in Chrome on Mac?
faq.answer: Google's help pages do not describe one. Chrome's developer docs describe the autoplay policy and document no user-facing toggle. The closest documented control is the Sounds setting, which you change one site at a time.

faq.question: Why does a muted video still play on its own?
faq.answer: Chrome always allows muted autoplay. Blocking or muting sound only changes what you hear. It does not stop the video from starting on the page.

faq.question: When does Chrome allow autoplay with sound?
faq.answer: Chrome allows it after you have interacted with the site. It also allows it when the desktop Media Engagement Index threshold is crossed, or for an installed PWA on desktop.

faq.question: What counts toward the Media Engagement Index?
faq.answer: A playback must last over 7 seconds, have unmuted audio, run in an active tab, and show a video larger than 200x140 px. Chrome's developer blog lists these limits.

faq.question: Should I install the Disable HTML5 Autoplay extension?
faq.answer: I did not verify that it is current. Read its listing, its permissions, and its reviews before you install it. Remove it if it breaks video playback on sites you use.

faq.question: What do the permission prompt choices mean?
faq.answer: Google's help page lists three choices: Allow this time, Allow while visiting the site, and Never allow. Read each label before you click.

faq.question: Will these steps work in Safari or Firefox?
faq.answer: This guide covers Google Chrome on macOS only. The menu names come from Google's Chrome Help pages, so other browsers will label things differently.

faq.question: Why does my Mac need macOS 13 for Chrome?
faq.answer: Google lists macOS 13 Ventura and later as the minimum for Chrome on Mac. Its requirements page gives no date for that rule, so check it again before you upgrade.

steps.name: Open Chrome Settings
steps.text: Click More, the three-dot icon at the top right of the Chrome window. Choose Settings. You can also press ⌘ , to open Settings in a new tab.
steps.tip: Settings opens in a new tab, so the page you are on stays open.

steps.name: Open Privacy and security
steps.text: In the left column, choose Privacy and security. Google's help page places Site settings inside this section.
steps.tip: Google's full path is More > Settings > Privacy and security > Site settings. Use that order if your labels differ.

steps.name: Open Site settings
steps.text: Choose Site settings. The page lists the permissions Chrome controls for websites. Find the entry named Sounds. Google's help page says it controls whether sites can play audio for music, videos, and other media.
steps.tip: You only need the Sounds entry. Skip the other permissions for this fix.

steps.name: Open the site you want to change
steps.text: Load the site in a tab. Click the icon to the left of the address. Google calls it View site information. Choose Site settings from that panel.
steps.tip: Changes save automatically, so there is no Save button to find.

steps.name: Set Sounds to block audio
steps.text: Find Sounds in the site's settings. Open its menu and choose the option that stops the site from playing audio. Google's help page does not list the option names, so read them before you pick.
steps.tip: Third-party guides use the names Mute and Automatic (default). Those labels may not match your version.

steps.name: Reload and test the video
steps.text: Close the settings tab and return to the page. Reload it, then start the video. You should hear nothing from the site. The picture may still move, because Chrome always allows muted autoplay.

steps.name: Repeat for each site
steps.text: Chrome has no documented switch that covers every site at once. Repeat the site and Sounds steps for each one that starts video on its own. Keep a short list so you do not check the same site twice.
steps.tip: Note the sites that still play sound after you change the setting. Those need the player or extension options.

shortcuts.action: Open Settings in a new tab

troubleshooting.problem: The video starts, but no sound comes out.
troubleshooting.fix: That is expected when muted autoplay is allowed. Blocking sound is the setting that works here. Stopping the picture needs the site's player or an extension.

troubleshooting.problem: I cannot find Sounds in Site settings.
troubleshooting.fix: Check the full path: More > Settings > Privacy and security > Site settings. If it is still missing, confirm your Mac runs macOS 13 Ventura or later, the minimum Google lists for Chrome on Mac.

troubleshooting.problem: Other sites still start videos on their own.
troubleshooting.fix: Chrome has no documented switch for all sites. Repeat the site and Sounds steps for each one, then check each site's own player for an autoplay control.

troubleshooting.problem: Chrome's menus look different from this guide.
troubleshooting.fix: Labels can change between releases. Follow the path in order and choose the closest match. Skip any guide that mentions Flash or Chrome > Preferences, since it predates current Chrome.

troubleshooting.problem: A site plays with sound after you use it for a while.
troubleshooting.fix: Chrome may have counted enough engagement for that site. A playback counts only if it lasts over 7 seconds with unmuted audio in an active tab. You can view your index at about://media-engagement.
